content.text: When you take ice cubes out of the freezer, they slowly melt into liquid water. When you boil a kettle, the water turns into steam. When you hang wet clothes on a washing line, they dry even on a cool day without the water ever boiling. These three processes, melting, boiling, and evaporation, are all changes of state, but they are fundamentally different in how they occur and what drives them. Understanding these differences is essential to making sense of many everyday phenomena, from weather patterns to how your body cools itself through sweating.
In this lesson, we will explore the physics of melting, boiling, and evaporation in detail, using the particle model to explain what happens at each stage.

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. As the solid is heated, the particles vibrate more and more vigorously. At the melting point, the particles have enough kinetic energy to partially overcome the attractive forces between them. They begin to break free from their fixed positions and slide past one another. The solid becomes a liquid.

During melting, the temperature remains constant even though energy is still being supplied. This is because the energy is being used to break the bonds between particles (increasing their potential energy) rather than to increase their kinetic energy. Since temperature depends on kinetic energy, the temperature stays the same until all the solid has melted.
is the rapid change from liquid to gas that occurs at a specific temperature called the
. Like the melting point, the boiling point of a pure substance at a given pressure is a fixed temperature.
It occurs throughout the entire liquid, not just at the surface.
It occurs at a specific, fixed temperature (the boiling point).
Bubbles of vapour form within the liquid and rise to the surface.
It requires a continuous supply of energy.
The temperature remains constant during boiling.

At the boiling point, particles throughout the liquid have enough energy to completely overcome the forces of attraction between them. They escape from the liquid in all directions, forming bubbles of vapour that rise to the surface. Energy is used to break the remaining bonds between particles, so the temperature remains constant until all the liquid has boiled away.
Effect of pressure on boiling point:

The boiling point depends on the external pressure. At higher pressures, it is harder for particles to escape from the liquid, so a higher temperature (more energy) is needed. The boiling point increases. At lower pressures, particles can escape more easily, so the boiling point decreases.

In a liquid, particles have a range of kinetic energies. Most particles have moderate energy, but some have much more than average and some have much less. At the surface of the liquid, some of the faster-moving particles have enough energy to escape from the surface and become gas particles. These are the particles with the highest kinetic energy.

As the most energetic particles leave, the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles decreases. Since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, the temperature of the remaining liquid drops. This is why evaporation causes cooling.

| Feature | Evaporation | Boiling |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Temperature | Occurs at any temperature | Occurs only at the boiling point |
| Location | Surface of the liquid only | Throughout the entire liquid |
| Speed | Slow, gradual process | Rapid, vigorous process |
| Bubbles | No bubbles formed | Bubbles of vapour form within the liquid |
| Energy source | Takes energy from the liquid itself (cooling) | Requires external energy supply |
| Temperature change | Liquid cools down | Temperature remains constant |

It is important to understand that both evaporation and boiling involve the same fundamental process: particles gaining enough energy to escape from the liquid phase. The difference is that in boiling, this happens throughout the liquid because all particles have at least the minimum energy needed, while in evaporation, only the fastest particles at the surface can escape.
Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation
Several factors increase the rate of evaporation:
At higher temperatures, a greater proportion of particles have enough energy to escape from the surface. This is why wet clothes dry faster on a warm day.
A larger surface area means more particles are at the surface and have the opportunity to escape. Water in a wide, shallow dish evaporates faster than the same volume in a narrow, deep container.

When a particle escapes from the liquid surface, it enters the air just above the surface. If the air is still, these escaped particles may collide with air molecules and bounce back into the liquid. Moving air carries these escaped particles away, preventing them from returning. This allows more particles to escape. This is why wet clothes dry faster on a windy day and why you feel cooler when a fan blows air over your skin.

If the air already contains a lot of water vapour (high humidity), fewer water molecules can escape into it because some water vapour molecules will return to the liquid. On a dry day, evaporation is faster because the air can accept more water molecules.
At lower pressures, there are fewer air molecules above the surface pushing particles back into the liquid, so evaporation is faster.
The cooling effect of evaporation is one of the most important concepts in this lesson. It explains many everyday phenomena:

When your body gets hot, sweat glands produce liquid sweat on your skin. As the sweat evaporates, it takes energy from your skin, cooling you down. On a humid day, sweat evaporates more slowly, which is why you feel hotter and more uncomfortable.
When you get out of a swimming pool, the water on your skin evaporates. The energy for evaporation comes from your skin, making you feel cold. This effect is stronger on a windy day.

In a refrigerator, a volatile liquid (refrigerant) is allowed to evaporate inside coils at the back of the fridge compartment. As it evaporates, it absorbs heat from inside the fridge, cooling the contents. The vapour is then compressed back into a liquid and the cycle repeats.
Cooling drinks with a wet cloth:
Wrapping a wet cloth around a bottle and placing it in a breeze cools the drink. The evaporating water takes energy from the bottle, lowering the temperature of the drink inside.

A student dips their hand in water and then waves it in the air. Explain why their hand feels cold.

The water on the student's hand evaporates. In the liquid water, particles have a range of kinetic energies. The particles with the highest kinetic energy are the ones most likely to escape from the surface. When these fast-moving particles leave, the average kinetic energy of the remaining water particles decreases. Since temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, the water remaining on the hand becomes colder. Energy is transferred from the hand to the water to replace the lost energy, making the hand feel cold.

Waving the hand in the air increases the rate of evaporation by moving air across the surface, removing water vapour and allowing more particles to escape. This makes the cooling effect even stronger.

Two identical saucers each contain 10 mL of water. Saucer A is placed in a warm room with a fan blowing across it. Saucer B is placed in a cool, still room. Which saucer's water will evaporate first? Explain each factor.
Saucer A will evaporate first. There are two factors at play:
The water molecules have more kinetic energy on average. A larger proportion of molecules at the surface have enough energy to escape, so evaporation is faster.

The fan blows away water vapour from just above the liquid surface. This prevents escaped molecules from returning to the liquid and maintains a low concentration of water vapour near the surface, allowing more molecules to escape.
Both factors increase the rate of evaporation for saucer A compared to saucer B.
Worked Example 4: Pressure and Boiling Point
A mountaineer is camping at high altitude where the atmospheric pressure is very low. She finds that she cannot cook her food properly by boiling it in water. Explain why, and suggest a solution.

At high altitude, the atmospheric pressure is lower than at sea level. This means that water molecules can escape from the liquid more easily (less atmospheric pressure pushing down on the surface). As a result, water boils at a lower temperature than
. At very high altitudes, water might boil at
Since the water boils at a lower temperature, it does not get hot enough to cook food properly. The food remains undercooked even though the water is boiling vigorously.

The mountaineer could use a pressure cooker. A pressure cooker seals in the steam, increasing the pressure above the liquid. This raises the boiling point, allowing the water to reach a higher temperature and cook the food properly.

Boiling and evaporation are different processes. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a specific temperature, while evaporation occurs only at the surface at any temperature. Boiling requires an external energy supply, while evaporation takes energy from the liquid itself.
Misconception 2: "Bubbles in boiling water contain air"

The bubbles that form during boiling contain water vapour (steam), not air. Small bubbles that appear before the water reaches boiling point are dissolved air being released, but the large, vigorous bubbles during boiling are pure water vapour.
Misconception 3: "Temperature always increases when you heat something"
During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though energy is being supplied. The energy goes into breaking bonds between particles, not into increasing kinetic energy.
Misconception 4: "Steam at 100°C is the same as water at 100°C"

Misconception 5: "Water can only evaporate when it is hot"
Evaporation occurs at any temperature, even near
. Wet clothes will eventually dry even on a cold day, although the process is slower than on a warm day.
Misconception 6: "Adding more heat always makes the temperature go up faster"
During a change of state, adding more heat does not increase the temperature at all. It only makes the change of state happen faster (more solid melts per second, or more liquid boils per second).
